name: Tamil
variety: Formal Tamil as read aloud by educated speakers from Tamil Nadu (the style described by Keane 2004), with notes on colloquial speech
sources: Keane, Elinor (2004). Tamil. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 34(1) (Illustrations of the IPA).
Schiffman, Harold F. (1999). A Reference Grammar of Spoken Tamil. Cambridge University Press.
Asher, R. E. (1985). Tamil. London: Croom Helm (Croom Helm Descriptive Grammars).
Annamalai, E. and Steever, Sanford B. (1998). Modern Tamil. In Steever (ed.), The Dravidian Languages. London: Routledge.
Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju (2003). The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge University Press.

McDonough, Joyce and Johnson, Keith (1997). Tamil liquids: an investigation into the basis of the contrast among five liquids in a dialect of Tamil. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 27.
Narayanan, Shrikanth; Byrd, Dani; Kaun, Abigail (1999). Geometry, kinematics, and acoustics of Tamil liquid consonants. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 106(4).
Lisker, Leigh and Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20.
Balasubramanian, T. (1980). Timing in Tamil. Journal of Phonetics 8.
Balasubramanian, T. (1981). Duration of vowels in Tamil. Journal of Phonetics 9.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the rhythm class hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Keane, Elinor (2006). Rhythmic characteristics of colloquial and formal Tamil. Language and Speech 49(3).
Keane, Elinor (2014). The intonational phonology of Tamil. In Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology II. Oxford University Press.
Féry, Caroline (2010). Indian languages as intonational 'phrase languages'. In Hasnain and Chaudhary (eds.), Problematizing Language Studies: Festschrift for Rama Kant Agnihotri. Delhi: Aakar Books.
contrasts: vowel length for all five vowel qualities
single versus geminate consonants (stops, nasals, laterals, glides)
dental versus retroflex stops; dental or alveolar versus retroflex nasal and lateral
five liquids: alveolar tap /ɾ/ (ர), alveolar trill /r/ (ற, merged with the tap by many speakers), alveolar lateral /l/, retroflex lateral /ɭ/, retroflex central approximant /ɻ/ (ழ)
stop voicing is not contrastive in the native vocabulary: [p t̪ ʈ tʃ k] and [b d̪ ɖ dʒ ɡ] are positional variants; voiced stops contrast only in loanwords, mostly word-initially
dental /n̪/ (ந) and alveolar /n/ (ன) are separate letters but are in near-complementary distribution (dental word-initially and before /t̪/, alveolar elsewhere)
/f z ʂ h/ belong to the loan vocabulary (Sanskrit, Perso-Arabic, English)
allophony: /k/ is [k] word-initially and when geminate, [ɡ] after a nasal, and a fricative [x], [ɣ] or [h] between vowels
/t̪/ is [t̪] word-initially and when geminate, [d̪] after a nasal, and [ð] or lax [d̪] between vowels
/ʈ/ is [ʈ] when geminate, [ɖ] after a nasal, and [ɖ] or a flap [ɽ] between vowels; it does not begin native words
/p/ is [p] word-initially and when geminate, [b] after a nasal, and [β] or [b] between vowels
/tʃ/ is [tʃ] when geminate and after a stop, [dʒ] after a nasal, [s] between vowels, and varies between [s] and [tʃ] word-initially
the written geminate ற்ற is an alveolar stop with trilled or fricated release [tːr] (plain alveolar [tː] in Sri Lanka, dental [t̪ː] in colloquial Indian Tamil); ன்ற is [ndr]

/ɻ/ is a frictionless retroflex approximant made with the tongue tip curled back, with a lowered third formant close to the second; many speakers, above all colloquially, replace it with [ɭ] (or [j] in some dialects)
short /u/ is unrounded [ɯ] word-finally and generally outside the first syllable (the over-short final 'kuṟṟiyalukaram')
short /a/ is centralised [ɐ] or [ʌ]; short vowels are less peripheral than long ones
/ai/ is shortened outside the first syllable and tends to [ɛ] or [ej]; colloquially final /ai/ is [e] or [ɛ]
word-initial /e eː/ may take a [j] on-glide and /o oː/ a [ʋ] on-glide
a nasal is homorganic with a following stop, and the stop is voiced: [ŋɡ], [ɲdʒ], [ɳɖ], [n̪d̪], [mb]
colloquial speech deletes word-final nasals and nasalises the vowel (maram 'tree' is [maɾã]) and drops or shortens unstressed medial vowels
phonotactics: native words do not begin with a retroflex consonant, with /r/, /ɾ/ or /l/, nor with /ŋ/; loanwords with initial r or l traditionally take a prothetic vowel
words end in a vowel or in one of the sonorants /m n ɳ ɾ l ɭ ɻ j/; a final obstruent takes the epenthetic short [ɯ]
medial clusters are mostly geminates or homorganic nasal plus stop; liquid plus stop or geminate also occurs (paːrkka)
initial clusters of loanwords are broken up by an epenthetic vowel in writing and careful speech
single and geminate stops contrast only between vowels or after a sonorant; the single stop there is voiced or lenited, the geminate voiceless

stress.type: no lexical stress; weak fixed prominence, not contrastive
stress.rule: A slight prominence falls on the first syllable of the word; no word pairs are distinguished by stress.
stress.cues: mostly phrase-level pitch (low start of the word or phrase with a rise to its end) and full, unreduced vowel quality in the first syllable; duration is reserved for the length contrast and intensity plays little part

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none as a category in formal speech; short vowels are centralised, non-initial /u/ is unrounded and /ai/ shortened; colloquial speech deletes some short medial vowels
rhythm.notes: Traditionally called syllable-timed, by some mora-timed; timing was studied by Balasubramanian (1980). Rhythm metrics do not classify it cleanly: the vocalic nPVI in Grabe and Low (2002, one speaker) is as high as in English or German, which reflects contrastive vowel length, and Keane (2006) shows that formal and colloquial Tamil differ on the metrics.

length.notes: Long vowels are roughly twice as long as short vowels (Balasubramanian 1981). Geminate stops are voiceless with a long closure, which together with the lack of voicing and lenition separates them from single stops between vowels.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Lisker and Abramson 1964 (word-initial stops in isolated words; voiced initial stops occur in loanwords only)

intonation.declarative: each non-final phrase (often one word with its suffixes) starts low and rises to a high at its right edge; the final phrase, usually the verb, falls to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the clitic -ā on the questioned word (on the verb when the whole sentence is questioned), with statement word order; the long clitic vowel carries a high or rising-falling pitch
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main pitch peak; the following material is lower and the utterance ends low
intonation.continuation: high boundary at the end of non-final phrases and of non-finite clauses
intonation.accent_shape: LH per phrase: low on the first syllable, rise to a phrase-final high; tones mark phrase edges, there are no pitch accents tied to stressed syllables
intonation.notes: Treated as a 'phrase language' by Féry (2010); Keane (2014) gives the autosegmental analysis. Focus raises the rise on the focused phrase and compresses what follows.

problems: ழ /ɻ/ is phoneme z., which calls the base voiced retroflex sibilant fricative [ʐ] (recordings voc/zh with zh_rfx noise) and only relabels it ɻ for IPA output, so the retroflex approximant is produced with friction
ர /ɾ/ imports base1/r, the English approximant [ɹ] (IPA output [mˈʌɹʌm] for மரம்), instead of an alveolar tap; only ற is a trill
single stops between vowels are plain voiced stops [ɡ d b]; the lenited allophones [x ɣ h], [ð], [β] are missing, most audibly for /k/
ன்ற is [nr] without the stop of [ndr] (என்று comes out as [enrʉ]), and ற்ற is [ʈr] with a retroflex stop instead of alveolar [tːr]
ந and ன are both the alveolar base n; there is no dental nasal, also not before dental stops
non-initial /ai/ is always the full diphthong aI with length 280, never shortened or monophthongised
stress is put on the first syllable with stress-accent settings (amplitude and length differences, unstressed a to V, u to U), although Tamil has no stress accent
good: positional stop voicing is implemented in ta_rules: voiceless word-initially and when geminate, voiced after nasals and between vowels, with a long exception list for loanwords
vowel length (short 110 to 130, long 250 to 300 in table units) and geminates (doubled consonant phonemes) are kept
retroflex stops, nasal and lateral are distinct from the dental and alveolar series
unstressed and final short u is centralised [ʉ], close to the unrounded final vowel; ச is [s] between vowels, [tʃː] when geminate and [dʒ] after ஞ்

notes: Tamil is diglossic. Text is normally written in the formal language, so a reading voice should follow formal pronunciation; the colloquial processes listed above are for reference. Sri Lankan Tamil keeps more of the older contrasts (alveolar [tː], distinct ற).
